passage:
Note from Jyoti, team lead, for my own records.
For three weeks Ankita has stayed late, scrolling job news with a tight face. On Tuesday she laughed and said, "It won't touch my work, it's just hype," and on Thursday she said she should quit and retrain. Both swings looked like the same worry to me, though I can't be sure. Today I sat with her and asked which part of her work she would miss if a tool did the rest. She named client calls and catching wrong numbers in reports. I suggested one hour a week to try the tools on real tasks, and to keep building depth in the client accounts she knows best. She took out a notebook and made a list. I'll check in on Friday.

qa.q: What did Ankita say she would miss if a tool did the rest?
qa.a: She named client calls and catching wrong numbers in reports.

qa.q: What might lie behind Ankita's swings between "it's just hype" and wanting to quit?
qa.a: Probably worry about her career. Jyoti reads both swings as the same worry but admits that cannot be sure.

qa.q: What plan did Jyoti suggest, and why does it make sense?
qa.a: One hour a week to try the tools on real tasks, plus building depth in the client accounts Ankita knows best. It faces the change without panic or denial.

qa.q: How might Ankita have experienced Jyoti's question about what she would miss?
qa.a: Perhaps as being taken seriously rather than brushed off, since she took out a notebook and made a list.

grounding: Fear that AI makes a career obsolete: neither panic nor denial, but learning the tools, focusing on judgement and domain depth, and upskilling.

passage:
"I translated forty pages this week," Nikita said, dropping onto the sofa. "Do you know how many the company's new AI tool did? Four hundred."

Urmila, her older sister, looked up from her laptop. "And?"

"And they'll replace us. Half the translators in my batch are already looking for other jobs. I can't sleep."

"What does the tool get wrong?"

Nikita laughed bitterly. "Everything that matters. Jokes. Legal tone. It translated a Marathi proverb about patience into something about cows."

"So who fixes that?"

"Me. Or someone like me."

Urmila closed her laptop. "Then learn the tool properly. Become the person who checks it, who knows the law and the culture better than any machine. Take that court-translation course you keep talking about."

Nikita was quiet. "That's less scary than just waiting."

"Waiting is the scary part," Urmila said.

That night Nikita filled in the course form.

qa.q: How many pages did Nikita translate that week?
What was Nikita feeling about the AI tool?
qa.a: She felt anxious and afraid of being replaced, so worried she couldn't sleep.

qa.q: What plan did Urmila help Nikita make?
qa.a: To learn the tool, focus on checking its work, deepen her legal and cultural knowledge, and take the court-translation course.

qa.q: How does Urmila see Nikita's fear?
qa.a: Urmila takes it seriously but sees waiting and panicking as the real danger, and pushes her toward action.

grounding: The dialogue shows someone who fears AI will make her career obsolete, and a sister helping her act by learning the tool, focusing on judgment and domain depth, and upskilling.

passage:
I'm Uday. Two years ago I was a junior graphic designer in Pune, and I was sure I'd be out of work by Diwali.

The image generators had arrived. Our clients were sending us things they'd made in five minutes and asking why we charged so much. For a month I did nothing but scroll horror stories. Then I swung the other way and told everyone the tools were useless. Both felt better than looking honestly.

Anjali, the senior designer, took me to lunch. "Panic and denial are both ways of doing nothing," she said.

So I made a plan. I learned the tools in the evenings. I spent time with our clients' real problems, what their customers needed, which is where I'm actually useful. I took a course in brand strategy.

Last month a client said, "The tool gave me fifty logos. You told me which one was right, and why." That's the part I'm betting on now.

qa.q: What did Anjali say about panic and denial?
qa.a: "Panic and denial are both ways of doing nothing."

qa.q: How did Uday feel in the month after the image generators arrived?
qa.a: Uday felt frightened and anxious about losing work, first scrolling horror stories and then denying the tools mattered.

qa.q: Which choices helped Uday most, and why?
qa.a: Learning the tools, focusing on clients' real problems and taking a brand strategy course, because they built judgment and depth the tools can't replace.

qa.q: How does the client see Uday's value?
qa.a: The client values Uday's judgment in choosing the right logo and explaining why, not just the making of options.

grounding: The reflective account shows someone who feared AI would make their career obsolete, moving past panic and denial by learning the tools and building judgment, relationships and domain depth.
